films.detail: I start with the maths map and the different explanations of the research, then Plectis Atlas, where you can read OpenAI's maths papers alongside other groups' checking reports. I also introduce One Checkout, Code Map and Safety Core, the tools I've been using with coding agents, and a Zenith experiment on whether showing a model its earlier mistakes helps it test new code. These are all prototypes, and the separate videos go into each project.

transcript.text: I go through the maths, the code map, how I make these videos, and the tools I use to manage the agents. Then some research into how the agents could improve their own way of working.

chapters.title: The average of a complete cycle

films.detail: I start with what an infinite sum means, then work through the example where the chosen exponents keep doubling. From there I explain the restriction on the remainder a fraction can leave, and how averaging lets us extend the argument to other choices. The condition is that adding one divided by each chosen exponent gives a finite total. I also go through where this method stops and how the result relates to the proof written in Lean.

transcript.text: Could a sum made from 1, 1/3, 1/7, 1/15, … be a fraction? I explain a condition from Erdős that rules this out for certain selections; the full question is still open.

Erdős problem 257 asks what happens when you choose infinitely many different entries from 1, 1/3, 1/7, 1/15, and so on, and add them. Must the total be irrational, meaning it cannot equal a fraction of two whole numbers? The full question is still open; in this video I explain a known partial result.

transcript.text: I show how to commit one fix while another agent's unfinished edits stay in the same file.

films.detail: I also explain how an old copy in Git's staging area can put the old login code back into the next commit, why the agent needs to test the version it's actually saving, and when Git worktrees with separate project folders might make more sense. The agent still has to choose the right edits, and One Checkout doesn't stop agents overwriting each other's work. It also skips Git hooks, so the project's required checks have to be run separately.
films.summary: Two AI coding assistants can edit the same file at the same time. I show how to save just the finished login fix as a Git commit while the other assistant’s unfinished edits stay in place.

transcript.text: Choose one finished code change to save while other agents’ unfinished edits stay in place. I use a login fix as the example, and there is a small demo you can try yourself.

The example is a finished login fix and an unfinished permissions change: I go through how to save just the fix in the project's history while leaving both edits in the working file.

films.title: Zenith: I showed an AI tester the bugs it missed
films.label: Zenith
films.description: I test whether an AI code tester catches more bugs after seeing a record of its earlier misses.

transcript.text: I test whether an AI code tester catches more bugs after seeing a record of its earlier misses.

chapters.title: Can past misses help an AI tester?

films.detail: On 58 new problems, the record of earlier misses improved the average share of bugs caught from about 69% to 77%. I go through where that gain came from, including inputs that made slow code exceed the time limit and inputs written in the right format. When I count only wrong answers and crashes, the remaining improvement could be chance. The rules didn't produce a clear improvement.

transcript.text: For this Zenith experiment, I gave an AI model a record of the bugs it had missed and tested whether that helped it catch bugs in new programs. In this video I explain the test using a program that crashes on an empty list, then compare giving the model its earlier misses with giving it rules written from those mistakes.

home.title: Plectis: projects by Will Cook
home.description: Tools and research by Will Cook for understanding the work AI produces. Explore the videos, code maps, mathematics, agent tools and their source.
home.heading: Plectis
home.lede: I’m Will Cook. I use AI to research Erdős problems, questions posed by the mathematician Paul Erdős, and I build tools that help people follow what AI produces.
home.orientation: Start with the introduction, or choose a project to find out more.
why: As AI produces more complicated code and research, following its work gets harder. I’m using AI to build explanations and interfaces that help people inspect that work.

I keep the research, papers, code and recordings together in my working system. An agent writing a short paper can read the long research record, and a coding agent can read the same saved file descriptions that I see in Code Map.

AI does much of the research and coding. I direct the work, record the explanations and review the results. When an agent edits a video, it can read my transcript alongside the papers and code. I’d like to develop this with researchers and lecturers who can judge the subject properly.

These videos show what I’ve learned to build. I’d love to put those skills to use on other problems. I’m looking for work, an internship, fellowship or funding, and I’m very open to working together. If there’s a problem you think I should try, please let me know.
home.invitation: If something doesn’t make sense, or you spot a mistake, please let me know. If your feedback leads to a change, I’d be happy to credit you, with your permission.

projects.name: Code Map
projects.purpose: Read saved descriptions of files and follow their recorded code connections in a map.
projects.detail: The map and the agent’s text command read the same description stored with the code. In the video, I follow the Find search box from its search function to the file that supplies the search text. The recorded connections can omit dependencies, and the descriptions still need checking against the code.
projects.status: Still in development in my private system. I'm in the process of open sourcing it.

projects.name: One Checkout
projects.purpose: Commit a selected change while other agents’ unfinished edits stay in the same files.
projects.detail: Two coding agents, Claude and Codex, are editing the same file. Claude supplies a patch containing a finished login fix. One Checkout applies it to the last saved version for review, while Codex’s unfinished permissions change stays in the shared file. The agents still have to select and test the right edits and coordinate their work. The tool warns when an older staged copy could undo the fix in a later commit.

projects.name: Plectis Mathematics
projects.purpose: Eight Erdős problems I researched with AI, with the papers, computer-checked proofs of partial results and the approaches that failed.
projects.detail: Use the map to find a stated result, the part of a paper that explains it, and links to its proof and checking record. The film follows problem 257 through the long research record, short specialist paper, explanation paper and video.
projects.status: Research on particular cases and related results. The original questions remain open where the problem pages say so.

links.label: Contributions to Formal Conjectures (merged and open)
Palomar (selected results and their recorded checks)

projects.name: Plectis Atlas
projects.purpose: Read OpenAI’s maths papers alongside the reports that outside groups wrote about their claims and proofs.
projects.detail: The film follows one paper about pi. MathVet and Carlos Toledo’s cert-machine give it different coverage labels, but their notes agree on the claim left out of the statement chosen for checking. Atlas links to the original reports; it has not repeated their checks.

projects.name: Safety Core
projects.purpose: Keep agent rules in one file and see which are written instructions and which have a program checking commands.
projects.detail: In one small test, an agent tried to get past a failing test by supplying a made-up setting. A check written for that workaround asked for approval on all six attempts that reached it; without approval, none ran. The experiment used one model and one project, and the check does not detect settings written into a file.
projects.status: A prototype for Claude Code. The commit experiment ran the agent with the hooks installed. A separate publishing example calls the hook directly to compare asking for approval with refusing a command; that example runs no agent and publishes nothing.

projects.name: Demo Take
projects.purpose: I record an explanation, then agents can read the transcript alongside the maths and code when editing the video.
projects.detail: An agent can compare a line of narration with the paper or code it describes before preparing the picture. I review the edit and give feedback, so the video can be revised when an explanation or visual is unclear.
projects.status: Still part of my private system. There isn't a standalone public repository yet.

projects.name: Zenith
projects.purpose: Experiments on whether records of past mistakes help AI models test and repair code.
projects.detail: In the film, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash tests 58 new coding problems after practising on 28. Giving it records of earlier misses raised the average share of distinct faults caught per problem from about 69% to 77%, with no retraining. Some of the increase came from timeouts and correctly formatted inputs; counting only wrong answers and crashes gave a smaller improvement that could be chance.
projects.status: Small research studies, with limits described in the repository. The film explains the experiment on learning from earlier missed bugs.
